title: No More Than Twelve
hook: Two hours in. One more parallel.
scene: Spokane, the sky still black over a city that kept some of its lights on, and the clock already past five. The checkpoint was two figures behind sawhorses and a posted speed you held. Now the sawhorse line is the curb: signal, reverse, look where the car is going, and back into the gap with paint on one side and Mom's quiet on the other. Twelve inches from the curb is the number the guide gives. One more, like the lot in Kent, forty times over.
decision: The car is in the gap. How close to the curb?

options.text: As close as the tires will go — tight is tidy.
options.result: You keep rolling for the last inch and the tire finds the paint and the curb finds the wheel. Tight is not tidy. Twelve inches is the number, and it is a maximum, not a challenge.

options.text: Stop a couple of feet out — the line is only paint.
options.result: Two feet out is a car sitting in the lane, not at the curb. The line is paint; the rule is twelve inches.

options.text: Roll it in on the brake so it settles faster.
options.result: You ride the brake into the gap and the car noses down and stops short of where you aimed. Reverse, look, and let it roll — the brake is for stopping, not for steering the last foot.

options.text: No more than twelve inches, rear wheel a hand off the paint, then stop.
options.result: You finish the roll with the rear wheel a hand off the paint, straighten it, and stop before the bumper behind you. Twelve inches is the guide's number, and a hand is a hand from the line.

debrief: A parallel park ends no more than twelve inches from the curb, straightened, stopped before the car behind you. The posted speed through the checkpoint is a limit for ideal conditions, and the last two hours are not ideal.

source.teaching_target: 4.18 parallel parking: 'Make sure your vehicle is no more than 12 inches from the curb.' 5.1: the posted limit is the maximum for ideal conditions.
